TRIGGER CORRECTED ON REPAIR: an earlier version asserted that a 9-month maximum 'matches no standard misdemeanor term in s. 775.082' -- a claim about the absence of a term in a source this table lists as unread. That assertion is withdrawn; this table makes no claim about the contents of 775.082.
rows.quote: b. Not more than 9 months for a second conviction.

rows.trigger: Second conviction. Mandatory ignition interlock for at least 1 year, contingent on the person qualifying for a permanent or restricted license. Not a degree provision but a mandatory consequence attached to a second conviction. NOTE the numbering trap inside (2)(a): subparagraph 1 is fines, subparagraph 2 is imprisonment, and subparagraph 3 is neither -- it is an interlock mandate. A reader who opens (2)(a) looking for the jail exposure, finds it in subparagraph 2, and stops will never reach subparagraph 3 or the flush paragraph that follows it.
rows.quote: 3. For a second conviction, by mandatory placement for a period of at least 1 year, at the convicted person’s sole expense, of an ignition interlock device approved by the department in accordance with s. 316.1938 upon all vehicles that are individually or jointly leased or owned and routinely operated by the convicted person, when the convicted person qualifies for a permanent or restricted license.

rows.trigger: Unnumbered paragraph closing (2)(a), carrying no cite of its own. It is a fiscal-disposition rule: the amount of a (2)(a)1. fine above the $500 / $1,000 floors goes to the Department of Revenue rather than to the local clerk. It does not change the fine ranges in 1.a. or 1.b. and assigns no degree. Parallel remittance sentences appear inside (2)(b)2., inside (2)(b)3., and in the flush language of subsection (4).
rows.quote: The portion of a fine imposed in excess of $500 pursuant to sub-subparagraph 1.a. and the portion of a fine imposed in excess of $1,000 pursuant to sub-subparagraph 1.b., shall be remitted by the clerk to the Department of Revenue for deposit into the General Revenue Fund.

rows.trigger: Third violation where the offense occurs WITHIN 10 years after a prior conviction. Level 3 independently re-verified this pass from the F.S. 921.0022(3)(c) LEVEL 3 chart, entry '316.193(2)(b) | 3rd | Felony DUI, 3rd conviction.' Also carries mandatory interlock of not less than 2 years.
rows.quote: Any person who is convicted of a third violation of this section for an offense that occurs within 10 years after a prior conviction for a violation of this section commits a felony of the third degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082, s. 775.083, or s. 775.084. In addition, the court shall order the mandatory placement for a period of not less than 2 years, at the convicted person’s sole expense, of an ignition interlock device approved by the department in accordance with s. 316.1938 upon all vehicles that are individually or jointly leased or owned and routinely operated by the convicted person, when the convicted person qualifies for a permanent or restricted license.

rows.trigger: THIS IS THE STOP-READING TRAP IN THIS SECTION. A third violation occurring MORE THAN 10 years after the prior conviction is NOT a felony. The statute prescribes a fine of $2,000 to $5,000 and imprisonment of not more than 12 months and names no degree at all. Anyone who opens (2)(b), reads subparagraph 1, and concludes 'third DUI = third degree felony' states the law wrongly for every defendant whose prior is older than 10 years. Mandatory interlock of at least 2 years still applies. Note also that this class sits OUTSIDE the (6)(c) 30-day mandatory-minimum window, which requires the offense to occur within 10 years of a prior -- see the (6)(c) row.
rows.quote: Any person who is convicted of a third violation of this section for an offense that occurs more than 10 years after the date of a prior conviction for a violation of this section shall be punished by a fine of not less than $2,000 or more than $5,000 and by imprisonment for not more than 12 months. The portion of a fine imposed in excess of $2,500 pursuant to this subparagraph shall be remitted by the clerk to the Department of Revenue for deposit into the General Revenue Fund. In addition, the court shall order the mandatory placement for a period of at least 2 years, at the convicted person’s sole expense, of an ignition interlock device approved by the department in accordance with s. 316.1938 upon all vehicles that are individually or jointly leased or owned and routinely operated by the convicted person, when the convicted person qualifies for a permanent or restricted license.

rows.trigger: Fourth or subsequent violation, REGARDLESS of when any prior conviction occurred -- the 10-year window in subparagraphs 1 and 2 does not apply here. Same degree as (2)(b)1. (third degree felony) but placed in a higher offense severity level: Level 6, independently re-verified this pass from the F.S. 921.0022(3)(f) LEVEL 6 chart, entry '316.193(2)(b) | 3rd | Felony DUI, 4th or subsequent conviction.' The level numbers are ordinal chart placements, not a ratio scale, and this table does not read s. 921.0024 to compute point values. Fine floor is stated permissively ('may be not less than $2,000'), which is ambiguous on its face as to whether the $2,000 floor is mandatory.
rows.quote: Any person who is convicted of a fourth or subsequent violation of this section, regardless of when any prior conviction for a violation of this section occurred, commits a felony of the third degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082, s. 775.083, or s. 775.084. However, the fine imposed for such fourth or subsequent violation may be not less than $2,000. The portion of a fine imposed in excess of $1,000 pursuant to this subparagraph shall be remitted by the clerk to the Department of Revenue for deposit into the General Revenue Fund.

rows.trigger: Discretionary ('may order') interlock of at least 6 continuous months where the person's blood- or breath-alcohol level was .08 or higher at the time of the offense. Note this sets no minimum number of prior convictions, so it can reach a first offense.
rows.quote: In addition to the penalties in paragraph (a), the court may order placement, at the convicted person’s sole expense, of an ignition interlock device approved by the department in accordance with s. 316.1938 for at least 6 continuous months upon all vehicles that are individually or jointly leased or owned and routinely operated by the convicted person if, at the time of the offense, the person had a blood-alcohol level or breath-alcohol level of .08 or higher.

rows.trigger: Requires all three of (3)(a) violation of subsection (1), (3)(b) operating a vehicle, and (3)(c) causing or contributing to causing damage to the property OR the person of another. Note 'contributes to causing' -- sole causation is not required. Not ranked in the F.S. 921.0022 chart, which covers felonies only.
rows.quote: Any person:(a) Who is in violation of subsection (1);(b) Who operates a vehicle; and (c) Who, by reason of such operation, causes or contributes to causing:1. Damage to the property or person of another commits a misdemeanor of the first degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082 or s. 775.083.

rows.trigger: Causes or contributes to causing serious bodily injury to another, as that term is defined in s. 316.1933. No prior conviction required -- a first-time offender falls here. Level 7 independently re-verified this pass from the F.S. 921.0022(3)(g) LEVEL 7 chart, entry '316.193(3)(c)2. | 3rd | DUI resulting in serious bodily injury.'
rows.quote: Serious bodily injury to another, as defined in s. 316.1933, commits a felony of the third degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082, s. 775.083, or s. 775.084.

rows.trigger: Causes or contributes to causing the death of any human being OR unborn child ('unborn child' has the meaning in s. 775.021(5)). No prior conviction required. Level 8 independently re-verified this pass from the F.S. 921.0022(3)(h) LEVEL 8 chart, entry '316.193 (3)(c)3.a. | 2nd | DUI manslaughter.' Subject to the 4-year mandatory minimum in the flush language at the end of subsection (3).
rows.quote: The death of any human being or unborn child commits DUI manslaughter, and commits:a. A felony of the second degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082, s. 775.083, or s. 775.084.

rows.trigger: DUI manslaughter elevated one degree where BOTH conditions are met: the person knew or should have known the crash occurred, AND the person failed to give information and render aid under s. 316.062. Both (I) and (II) are required -- they are joined by 'and'. Level 9 independently re-verified this pass from the F.S. 921.0022(3)(i) LEVEL 9 chart, entry '316.193 (3)(c)3.b. | 1st | DUI manslaughter; failing to render aid or give information.'
rows.quote: b. A felony of the first degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082, s. 775.083, or s. 775.084, if:(I) At the time of the crash, the person knew, or should have known, that the crash occurred; and (II) The person failed to give information and render aid as required by s. 316.062.

rows.trigger: DUI manslaughter elevated one degree by criminal history: a prior conviction under this same subparagraph (DUI manslaughter), or under s. 327.35(3)(a)3.c. (BUI manslaughter), s. 782.071 (vehicular homicide), or s. 782.072 (vessel homicide). Level 9 independently re-verified this pass from the F.S. 921.0022(3)(i) LEVEL 9 chart, entry '316.193 (3)(c)3.c. | 1st | DUI manslaughter; prior conviction for DUI manslaughter, BUI manslaughter, vehicular homicide, or vessel homicide.' QUOTE CLEANED ON REPAIR: the source HTML prints a superscript editor's-footnote marker immediately before 's. 327.35(3)(a)3.c.'; that marker is editorial apparatus, not operative text, and is omitted from the quote. The footnote states the citation was substituted by the editors for a reference to s. 327.35(3)(c)3. to conform to a 2025 redesignation of subunits in s. 327.35.
rows.quote: c. A felony of the first degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082, s. 775.083, or s. 775.084, if the person has a prior conviction under this subparagraph, s. 327.35(3)(a)3.c., s. 782.071, or s. 782.072.

rows.trigger: Unnumbered flush paragraph closing subsection (3). Easy to miss because it sits after the last sub-subparagraph and carries no cite of its own. It imposes a 4-year mandatory minimum on EVERY DUI manslaughter conviction, i.e. on 3.a., 3.b., and 3.c. alike, and supplies the definition of 'unborn child'. Note it does NOT reach (3)(c)1. or (3)(c)2., which are not DUI manslaughter.
rows.quote: For purposes of this subsection, the term “unborn child” has the same meaning as provided in s. 775.021(5). A person who is convicted of DUI manslaughter shall be sentenced to a mandatory minimum term of imprisonment of 4 years.

rows.trigger: Enhanced penalty subsection, triggered by EITHER a blood- or breath-alcohol level of 0.15 or higher OR being accompanied in the vehicle by a person under 18 at the time of the offense. It raises fines and jail terms but assigns NO degree -- an enhanced first offense is still not made a felony by this subsection. First conviction fine range. SCOPE RETYPED ON REPAIR: this row previously carried scope null while its siblings (4)(a)2. and (4)(a)3. carried 'prior', splitting a single conviction-count axis inside one paragraph. Every conviction-count tier in this table, including first-conviction tiers, now uniformly carries scope 'prior'.
rows.quote: Any person who is convicted of a violation of subsection (1) and who has a blood-alcohol level or breath-alcohol level of 0.15 or higher, or any person who is convicted of a violation of subsection (1) and who at the time of the offense was accompanied in the vehicle by a person under the age of 18 years, shall be punished:(a) By a fine of:1. Not less than $1,000 or more than $2,000 for a first conviction.

rows.trigger: Second conviction under the 0.15-or-higher / minor-passenger enhancement. Fine range only, no degree. Per the flush language following (4)(b)2., the prior conviction that puts a defendant in this tier need NOT itself have been a 0.15-or-higher offense.
rows.quote: 2. Not less than $2,000 or more than $4,000 for a second conviction.

rows.trigger: Third or subsequent conviction under the enhancement. CRITICAL: this fine has a floor of $4,000 and NO STATED CEILING -- unlike (a)1. and (a)2. it prescribes 'not less than' with no upper bound. It also assigns no degree, so a third or subsequent offense is still graded by (2)(b), not here.
rows.quote: 3. Not less than $4,000 for a third or subsequent conviction.

rows.trigger: First conviction under the 0.15-or-higher / minor-passenger enhancement. Term prescribed directly, no degree named. SCOPE RETYPED ON REPAIR: previously null while (4)(b)2. carried 'prior'; the conviction-count axis is criminal history and is now typed 'prior' uniformly, first-conviction tiers included. See the separate row for the flush language following (4)(b)2. for the scope rule that governs this paragraph.
rows.quote: (b) By imprisonment for:1. Not more than 9 months for a first conviction.

rows.trigger: Second conviction under the enhancement. Term prescribed directly, no degree named. Note (4)(b) stops at a second conviction -- it prescribes NO jail term for a third or subsequent conviction, even though (4)(a)3. prescribes a fine for one. That asymmetry is on the face of the text.
rows.quote: 2. Not more than 12 months for a second conviction.

rows.trigger: Unnumbered paragraph sitting between (4)(b)2. and paragraph (4)(c), so it is visually easy to read past on the way to (c). Two independent rules. FIRST, a scope rule for the whole of subsection (4): 'only the instant offense is required to be a violation of subsection (1) by a person who has a blood-alcohol level or breath-alcohol level of 0.15 or higher.' That means the prior convictions that push a defendant into the (4)(a)2., (4)(a)3., and (4)(b)2. tiers need NOT themselves have been 0.15-or-higher offenses. Note on its face this sentence is written only in terms of the 0.15 trigger and says nothing express about the minor-passenger trigger; the statute does not resolve that asymmetry. SECOND, a fiscal-disposition rule remitting the above-floor portion of (4)(a) fines to the Department of Revenue.
rows.quote: For the purposes of this subsection, only the instant offense is required to be a violation of subsection (1) by a person who has a blood-alcohol level or breath-alcohol level of 0.15 or higher. The portion of a fine imposed in excess of $1,000 pursuant to subparagraph (a)1. and the portion of a fine imposed in excess of $2,000 pursuant to subparagraph (a)2. or subparagraph (a)3., shall be remitted by the clerk to the Department of Revenue for deposit into the General Revenue Fund.

rows.trigger: Mandatory ('shall order'), not discretionary: interlock for not less than 6 continuous months on a first offense and not less than 2 continuous years on a second offense, where the 0.15-or-higher or minor-passenger trigger is met. Contrast (2)(c), which is discretionary. The interlock DURATIONS vary by offense count, but the operative trigger of the paragraph is the enhancement condition, so this row is typed like its (2)(c) counterpart rather than as a conviction-count tier. Note this paragraph sits AFTER the subsection (4) flush language in the printed text.
rows.quote: In addition to the penalties in paragraphs (a) and (b), the court shall order the mandatory placement, at the convicted person’s sole expense, of an ignition interlock device approved by the department in accordance with s. 316.1938 upon all vehicles that are individually or jointly leased or owned and routinely operated by the convicted person for not less than 6 continuous months for the first offense and for not less than 2 continuous years for a second offense, when the convicted person qualifies for a permanent or restricted license.

rows.trigger: The single broadest penalty provision in the section: it reaches EVERY offender convicted of violating this section, including the (2)(b) and (3)(c) felonies, with no prior-conviction threshold and no BAC threshold. Three mandatory commands: the court SHALL place all such offenders on monthly reporting probation; the court SHALL require completion of a substance abuse course conducted by a DUI program licensed under s. 322.292, including a psychosocial evaluation; and where the program refers the offender to treatment, completion of the education, evaluation, and treatment is a condition of that probation, in addition to any sentence or fine. A treatment referral resulting from a psychosocial evaluation may not be waived without a supporting independent psychosocial evaluation by a court-appointed provider. On failure to report for or complete treatment or the education course and evaluation, the department SHALL cancel the driving privilege 'notwithstanding the terms of the court order or any suspension or revocation' -- an administrative consequence that overrides the sentencing court. Assigns no degree.
rows.quote: The court shall place all offenders convicted of violating this section on monthly reporting probation and shall require completion of a substance abuse course conducted by a DUI program licensed by the department under s. 322.292, which must include a psychosocial evaluation of the offender. If the DUI program refers the offender to an authorized substance abuse treatment provider for substance abuse treatment, in addition to any sentence or fine imposed under this section, completion of all such education, evaluation, and treatment is a condition of reporting probation. The offender shall assume reasonable costs for such education, evaluation, and treatment. The referral to treatment resulting from a psychosocial evaluation shall not be waived without a supporting independent psychosocial evaluation conducted by an authorized substance abuse treatment provider appointed by the court, which shall have access to the DUI program’s psychosocial evaluation before the independent psychosocial evaluation is conducted. The court shall review the results and recommendations of both evaluations before determining the request for waiver. The offender shall bear the full cost of this procedure. The term “substance abuse” means the abuse of alcohol or any substance named or described in Schedules I through V of s. 893.03. If an offender referred to treatment under this subsection fails to report for or complete such treatment or fails to complete the DUI program substance abuse education course and evaluation, the DUI program shall notify the court and the department of the failure. Upon receipt of the notice, the department shall cancel the offender’s driving privilege, notwithstanding the terms of the court order or any suspension or revocation of the driving privilege. The department may temporarily reinstate the driving privilege on a restricted basis upon verification from the DUI program that the offender is currently participating in treatment and the DUI education course and evaluation requirement has been completed. If the DUI program notifies the department of the second failure to complete treatment, the department shall reinstate the driving privilege only after notice of completion of treatment from the DUI program. The organization that conducts the substance abuse education and evaluation may not provide required substance abuse treatment unless a waiver has been granted to that organization by the department. A waiver may be granted only if the department determines, in accordance with its rules, that the service provider that conducts the substance abuse education and evaluation is the most appropriate service provider and is licensed under chapter 397 or is exempt from such licensure. A statistical referral report shall be submitted quarterly to the department by each organization authorized to provide services under this section.

rows.trigger: Subsection (6) applies 'regardless of any penalty imposed pursuant to subsection (2), subsection (3), or subsection (4)' -- these are additive to every grading provision above, including the felonies. First conviction: mandatory probation not to exceed 1 year; minimum 50 hours public service or community work; a $10-per-hour buyout available ONLY on an undue-hardship finding based on residence, location, or employment obligations; a cap that the total period of probation and incarceration may not exceed 1 year; and mandatory 10-day impoundment or immobilization. The impoundment reach here is NARROWER than in (6)(b) and (6)(c): this paragraph reaches only 'the vehicle that was operated by or in the actual control of the defendant or any one vehicle registered in the defendant's name' -- one vehicle. (6)(b) and (6)(c) reach ALL vehicles owned by the defendant. Impoundment must not run concurrently with incarceration, and the order may be dismissed under (6)(e), (f), (g), or (h) -- and, per (6)(i), on proof of installed interlock. No degree assigned.
rows.quote: With respect to any person convicted of a violation of subsection (1), regardless of any penalty imposed pursuant to subsection (2), subsection (3), or subsection (4):(a) For the first conviction, the court shall place the defendant on probation for a period not to exceed 1 year and, as a condition of such probation, shall order the defendant to participate in public service or a community work project for a minimum of 50 hours. The court may order a defendant to pay a fine of $10 for each hour of public service or community work otherwise required only if the court finds that the residence or location of the defendant at the time public service or community work is required or the defendant’s employment obligations would create an undue hardship for the defendant. However, the total period of probation and incarceration may not exceed 1 year. The court must also, as a condition of probation, order the impoundment or immobilization of the vehicle that was operated by or in the actual control of the defendant or any one vehicle registered in the defendant’s name at the time of impoundment or immobilization, for a period of 10 days or for the unexpired term of any lease or rental agreement that expires within 10 days. The impoundment or immobilization must not occur concurrently with the incarceration of the defendant. The impoundment or immobilization order may be dismissed in accordance with paragraph (e), paragraph (f), paragraph (g), or paragraph (h).

rows.trigger: MANDATORY MINIMUM JAIL, and note the window here is 5 years, NOT the 10 years used in (2)(b). A second conviction within 5 years of a prior carries a floor of 10 days imprisonment with at least 48 hours consecutive, plus 30-day impoundment of ALL vehicles owned by the defendant (broader than (6)(a), which reaches one vehicle). The differing time windows across (2)(b), (6)(b), and (6)(c) are a frequent source of error. Dismissal grounds are in (6)(e) through (6)(h) and, separately, (6)(i).
rows.quote: For the second conviction for an offense that occurs within a period of 5 years after the date of a prior conviction for violation of this section, the court shall order imprisonment for not less than 10 days. The court must also, as a condition of probation, order the impoundment or immobilization of all vehicles owned by the defendant at the time of impoundment or immobilization, for a period of 30 days or for the unexpired term of any lease or rental agreement that expires within 30 days. The impoundment or immobilization must not occur concurrently with the incarceration of the defendant and must occur concurrently with the driver license revocation imposed under s. 322.28(2)(a)2. The impoundment or immobilization order may be dismissed in accordance with paragraph (e), paragraph (f), paragraph (g), or paragraph (h). At least 48 hours of confinement must be consecutive.

rows.trigger: MANDATORY MINIMUM JAIL of not less than 30 days for a third or subsequent conviction for an offense that occurs WITHIN 10 years after the date of a prior conviction, with at least 48 hours consecutive, plus 90-day impoundment of ALL vehicles owned by the defendant (broader than (6)(a)). REACH CORRECTED ON REPAIR: an earlier version claimed this floor also reaches the (2)(b)2. non-felony third conviction. It does not. (6)(c) requires the offense to occur WITHIN 10 years after a prior conviction; (2)(b)2. requires it to occur MORE THAN 10 years after -- complementary conditions keyed to the identical 10-year window, so a defendant in the (2)(b)2. class is by definition outside (6)(c). And a third conviction that IS within 10 years of a prior is the (2)(b)1. felony, not (2)(b)2. What (6)(c) actually reaches: the (2)(b)1. third-conviction felony class, and the subset of (2)(b)3. fourth-or-subsequent felons whose instant offense falls within 10 years of a prior conviction ((2)(b)3. itself has no window, so a (2)(b)3. defendant whose priors are all older than 10 years is graded as a felon but sits outside this 30-day floor). Dismissal grounds are in (6)(e) through (6)(h) and, separately, (6)(i).
rows.quote: For the third or subsequent conviction for an offense that occurs within a period of 10 years after the date of a prior conviction for violation of this section, the court shall order imprisonment for not less than 30 days. The court must also, as a condition of probation, order the impoundment or immobilization of all vehicles owned by the defendant at the time of impoundment or immobilization, for a period of 90 days or for the unexpired term of any lease or rental agreement that expires within 90 days. The impoundment or immobilization must not occur concurrently with the incarceration of the defendant and must occur concurrently with the driver license revocation imposed under s. 322.28(2)(a)3. The impoundment or immobilization order may be dismissed in accordance with paragraph (e), paragraph (f), paragraph (g), or paragraph (h). At least 48 hours of confinement must be consecutive.

rows.trigger: Mechanics of the impoundment order required by (6)(a), (b), and (c). The court MUST issue the order at the time of sentencing; the order must list the name and telephone numbers of all immobilization agencies meeting the conditions of subsection (13); and within 7 business days the clerk must give certified-mail notice to any registered owner other than the defendant and to each lienholder of record. Assigns no degree, but it is the procedural predicate for the third-party dismissal rights in (e) through (h).
rows.quote: The court must at the time of sentencing the defendant issue an order for the impoundment or immobilization of a vehicle. The order of impoundment or immobilization must include the name and telephone numbers of all immobilization agencies meeting all of the conditions of subsection (13). Within 7 business days after the date that the court issues the order of impoundment or immobilization, the clerk of the court must send notice by certified mail, return receipt requested, to the registered owner of each vehicle, if the registered owner is a person other than the defendant, and to each person of record claiming a lien against the vehicle.

rows.trigger: First of the four dismissal grounds cross-referenced by name in (6)(a), (b), and (c). PARTY: this right belongs to a person who owns but was NOT operating the vehicle -- a non-defendant owner. SCOPE RETYPED ON REPAIR: the previous value 'non-defendant vehicle owner' is outside the typed vocabulary (dwelling/item/prior/victim/place), which has no value for party identity; the party is stated here in prose instead. The owner may submit a police report showing the vehicle was stolen at the time of the offense, or documentation of purchase after the offense from someone other than the defendant or the defendant's agent. On a finding of theft or a non-circumventing sale, the order MUST be dismissed and the owner incurs no costs. If the request is denied, the petitioner may request an evidentiary hearing.
rows.quote: A person who owns but was not operating the vehicle when the offense occurred may submit to the court a police report indicating that the vehicle was stolen at the time of the offense or documentation of having purchased the vehicle after the offense was committed from an entity other than the defendant or the defendant’s agent. If the court finds that the vehicle was stolen or that the sale was not made to circumvent the order and allow the defendant continued access to the vehicle, the order must be dismissed and the owner of the vehicle will incur no costs. If the court denies the request to dismiss the order of impoundment or immobilization, the petitioner may request an evidentiary hearing.

rows.trigger: Second dismissal ground, covering the case (e) does not. PARTY: a non-defendant owner who was not operating the vehicle (scope retyped to null on repair; party identity is off the typed vocabulary and lives here in prose). Covers the owner whose vehicle was stolen, or who bought it after the offense DIRECTLY from the defendant or the defendant's agent; such an owner may request an evidentiary hearing. Dismissal requires findings of theft, or of purchase without knowledge of the offense, plus no relationship to the defendant beyond the transaction, plus that the purchase would not circumvent the order.
rows.quote: A person who owns but was not operating the vehicle when the offense occurred, and whose vehicle was stolen or who purchased the vehicle after the offense was committed directly from the defendant or the defendant’s agent, may request an evidentiary hearing to determine whether the impoundment or immobilization should occur. If the court finds that either the vehicle was stolen or the purchase was made without knowledge of the offense, that the purchaser had no relationship to the defendant other than through the transaction, and that such purchase would not circumvent the order and allow the defendant continued access to the vehicle, the order must be dismissed and the owner of the vehicle will incur no costs.

rows.trigger: Third dismissal ground, and it is MANDATORY on the finding ('shall also dismiss'): the court must dismiss the impoundment or immobilization order if the family of the vehicle's owner has no other private or public means of transportation. Scope retyped to null on repair; the benefited party (the vehicle owner's family) is off the typed vocabulary and is stated here in prose.
rows.quote: The court shall also dismiss the order of impoundment or immobilization of the vehicle if the court finds that the family of the owner of the vehicle has no other private or public means of transportation.

rows.trigger: Fourth dismissal ground, and it is DISCRETIONARY ('may also dismiss'), unlike (g): vehicles owned by the defendant but operated solely by the defendant's employees or by employees of any business the defendant owns.
rows.quote: The court may also dismiss the order of impoundment or immobilization of any vehicles that are owned by the defendant but that are operated solely by the employees of the defendant or any business owned by the defendant.

rows.trigger: A FIFTH dismissal ground that the (6)(a), (b), and (c) cross-references do NOT list: those paragraphs name only (e), (f), (g), and (h), so a reader who follows only the cross-references will never reach it. Proof to the court's satisfaction of a functioning, certified ignition interlock device installed on all vehicles individually or jointly leased or owned and routinely operated by the convicted person lets the court dismiss the impoundment or immobilization order. Discretionary ('may also dismiss').
rows.quote: The court may also dismiss the order of impoundment or immobilization if the defendant provides proof to the satisfaction of the court that a functioning, certified ignition interlock device has been installed upon all vehicles that are individually or jointly leased or owned and routinely operated by the convicted person.

rows.trigger: Subparagraph 1 authorizes the court, 'notwithstanding the provisions of this section, s. 316.1937, and s. 322.2715 relating to ignition interlock devices required for second or subsequent offenders,' to order participation in a qualified sobriety and drug monitoring program IN ADDITION to the interlock requirement, at the person's sole expense. It is available both pretrial and posttrial. Subparagraph 2 defines the program and its permitted modalities (twice-daily breath testing; continuous transdermal monitoring in hardship cases; random blood, breath, urine, or oral fluid testing) and preserves the court's power to order an interlock as a testing modality. Subparagraph 3 defines 'evidence-based program' by a two-of-three test. Assigns no degree.
rows.quote: 1. Notwithstanding the provisions of this section, s. 316.1937, and s. 322.2715 relating to ignition interlock devices required for second or subsequent offenders, in order to strengthen the pretrial and posttrial options available to prosecutors and judges, the court may order, if deemed appropriate, that a person participate in a qualified sobriety and drug monitoring program, as defined in subparagraph 2., in addition to the ignition interlock device requirement. Participation shall be at the person’s sole expense. 2. As used in this paragraph, the term “qualified sobriety and drug monitoring program” means an evidence-based program, approved by the department, in which participants are regularly tested for alcohol and drug use. As the court deems appropriate, the program may monitor alcohol or drugs through one or more of the following modalities: breath testing twice a day; continuous transdermal alcohol monitoring in cases of hardship; or random blood, breath, urine, or oral fluid testing. Testing modalities that provide the best ability to sanction a violation as close in time as reasonably feasible to the occurrence of the violation should be given preference. This paragraph does not preclude a court from ordering an ignition interlock device as a testing modality. 3. For purposes of this paragraph, the term “evidence-based program” means a program that satisfies the requirements of at least two of the following:a. The program is included in the federal registry of evidence-based programs and practices.b. The program has been reported in a peer-reviewed journal as having positive effects on the primary targeted outcome.c. The program has been documented as effective by informed experts and other sources.

rows.trigger: Cost allocation for the impoundment or immobilization ordered under (6)(a), (b), and (c): all costs and fees, including the cost of the (6)(d) notification, fall on the vehicle's owner, or on the lessee or renter if leased or rented, UNLESS the order is dismissed under (e) through (i). Note this can put costs on a third-party owner who never drove. All provisions of s. 713.78 apply, and payment goes directly to the person impounding or immobilizing.
rows.quote: All costs and fees for the impoundment or immobilization, including the cost of notification, must be paid by the owner of the vehicle or, if the vehicle is leased or rented, by the person leasing or renting the vehicle, unless the impoundment or immobilization order is dismissed. All provisions of s. 713.78 shall apply. The costs and fees for the impoundment or immobilization must be paid directly to the person impounding or immobilizing the vehicle.

rows.trigger: Wrongful-taking remedy. PARTY: an owner or a lienholder of record who has NOT already sought review under (e), (f), or (g) (scope retyped to null on repair; party identity is off the typed vocabulary and lives here in prose). File a complaint within 10 days after knowledge of the vehicle's location, in the county of the owner's residence, to determine whether the vehicle was wrongfully taken or withheld. The vehicle can be released in the meantime by posting bond or security equal to the impoundment costs and fees. Note the text says 'impounded or immobilized under this paragraph' although the impoundment is ordered under paragraphs (a), (b), and (c).
rows.quote: The person who owns a vehicle that is impounded or immobilized under this paragraph, or a person who has a lien of record against such a vehicle and who has not requested a review of the impoundment pursuant to paragraph (e), paragraph (f), or paragraph (g), may, within 10 days after the date that person has knowledge of the location of the vehicle, file a complaint in the county in which the owner resides to determine whether the vehicle was wrongfully taken or withheld from the owner or lienholder. Upon the filing of a complaint, the owner or lienholder may have the vehicle released by posting with the court a bond or other adequate security equal to the amount of the costs and fees for impoundment or immobilization, including towing or storage, to ensure the payment of such costs and fees if the owner or lienholder does not prevail. When the bond is posted and the fee is paid as set forth in s. 28.24, the clerk of the court shall issue a certificate releasing the vehicle. At the time of release, after reasonable inspection, the owner or lienholder must give a receipt to the towing or storage company indicating any loss or damage to the vehicle or to the contents of the vehicle.

rows.trigger: This paragraph directly modifies HOW imprisonment prescribed anywhere in this section is served: in the court's discretion the defendant may serve 'all or any portion of a term of imprisonment to which the defendant has been sentenced pursuant to this section' in a residential alcoholism or residential drug abuse treatment program, and time in such a program MUST be credited toward the term. The text states NO carve-out. ENUMERATION CORRECTED ON REPAIR: an earlier version listed only (2)(a)2., (2)(b)2., (4)(b), and the (6)(b)/(6)(c) mandatory minimums, silently excluding every felony term. On its face the paragraph reaches every term imposed pursuant to this section: the misdemeanor-tier terms under (2)(a)2., (2)(b)2., and (4)(b); the (6)(b) and (6)(c) mandatory minimums; AND the felony terms imposed via s. 775.082 for (2)(b)1., (2)(b)3., and (3)(c)2., and all three DUI manslaughter grades in (3)(c)3., including the 4-year mandatory minimum in the subsection (3) flush language. Whether a court would in fact permit a DUI manslaughter mandatory minimum to be served in residential treatment is a construction question the face of the text does not resolve; the point recorded here is that the statute states no exception. Note it is buried at the very end of the (6) impoundment paragraphs, where nothing signals that it is about imprisonment generally rather than impoundment. Assigns no degree.
rows.quote: A defendant, in the court’s discretion, may be required to serve all or any portion of a term of imprisonment to which the defendant has been sentenced pursuant to this section in a residential alcoholism treatment program or a residential drug abuse treatment program. Any time spent in such a program must be credited by the court toward the term of imprisonment.

rows.trigger: Unnumbered paragraph closing subsection (6), easily missed. TWO distinct rules. FIRST, it defines what counts as a 'previous conviction' for the whole section and materially widens the prior-conviction triggers in (2)(a), (2)(b), (4), and (6): boating-under-the-influence convictions under s. 327.35, convictions under former s. 316.1931, former s. 860.01, and former s. 316.028, and ANY out-of-state alcohol- or drug-related traffic conviction all count as priors. SECOND, on a finding that the defendant is financially unable to pay all or part of a fine imposed under this section, the court may order additional public service or community work in lieu of the unpayable portion, valuing the services at not less than the federal minimum wage at the time of sentencing.
rows.quote: For the purposes of this section, any conviction for a violation of s. 327.35; a previous conviction for the violation of former s. 316.1931, former s. 860.01, or former s. 316.028; or a previous conviction outside this state for driving under the influence, driving while intoxicated, driving with an unlawful blood-alcohol level, driving with an unlawful breath-alcohol level, or any other similar alcohol-related or drug-related traffic offense, is also considered a previous conviction for violation of this section. However, in satisfaction of the fine imposed pursuant to this section, the court may, upon a finding that the defendant is financially unable to pay either all or part of the fine, order that the defendant participate for a specified additional period of time in public service or a community work project in lieu of payment of that portion of the fine which the court determines the defendant is unable to pay. In determining such additional sentence, the court shall consider the amount of the unpaid portion of the fine and the reasonable value of the services to be ordered; however, the court may not compute the reasonable value of services at a rate less than the federal minimum wage at the time of sentencing.

rows.trigger: Preserves civil exposure: a conviction under this section does not bar any civil suit for damages against the person convicted. Relevant to the total consequences of conviction and it assigns no degree.
rows.quote: A conviction under this section does not bar any civil suit for damages against the person so convicted.

rows.trigger: Clerk's arraignment-notice duty warning that on conviction the court SHALL suspend or revoke the driver license, plus the harmless-error rule: failure to give the notice does not affect the suspension or revocation. Note this is the only place in the section that states the license suspension or revocation consequence as a certainty ('shall'), and the operative suspension provisions live in chapter 322, not here.
rows.quote: At the arraignment, or in conjunction with any notice of arraignment provided by the clerk of the court, the clerk shall provide any person charged with a violation of this section with notice that upon conviction the court shall suspend or revoke the offender’s driver license and that the offender should make arrangements for transportation at any proceeding in which the court may take such action. Failure to provide such notice does not affect the court’s suspension or revocation of the offender’s driver license.

rows.trigger: A mandatory custodial consequence that attaches on ARREST, not on conviction, and so is missed by anyone reading only the conviction-keyed subsections. PARTY: the person arrested, pre-conviction (scope retyped to null on repair; 'arrestee' is off the typed vocabulary and lives here in prose). A person arrested for a violation of this section MAY NOT be released from custody until no longer impaired, until blood- or breath-alcohol is less than 0.05, or until 8 hours have elapsed from arrest. Note the paragraphs are joined by 'or', so the 8-hour paragraph functions as an outside limit rather than a floor that must be reached in every case. Assigns no degree.
rows.quote: A person who is arrested for a violation of this section may not be released from custody:(a) Until the person is no longer under the influence of alcoholic beverages, any chemical substance set forth in s. 877.111, or any substance controlled under chapter 893 and affected to the extent that his or her normal faculties are impaired;(b) Until the person’s blood-alcohol level or breath-alcohol level is less than 0.05; or (c) Until 8 hours have elapsed from the time the person was arrested.

rows.trigger: Evidentiary bar: DHSMV rulings under s. 322.2615 may not be considered in any trial under this section, and testimony or evidence from the administrative proceeding, or any written statement submitted in a request for administrative review, is inadmissible in any criminal proceeding unless timely disclosed in criminal discovery under Fla. R. Crim. P. 3.220. Assigns no degree.
rows.quote: The rulings of the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles under s. 322.2615 shall not be considered in any trial for a violation of this section. Testimony or evidence from the administrative proceedings or any written statement submitted by a person in his or her request for administrative review is inadmissible into evidence or for any other purpose in any criminal proceeding, unless timely disclosed in criminal discovery pursuant to Rule 3.220, Florida Rules of Criminal Procedure.

rows.trigger: Rulemaking directive to DHSMV to implement the use of ignition interlock devices, which are mandated or authorized by (2)(a)3., (2)(b)1., (2)(b)2., (2)(c), (4)(c), (6)(i), and (6)(j). Assigns no degree.
rows.quote: The Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles is directed to adopt rules providing for the implementation of the use of ignition interlock devices.

rows.trigger: Load-bearing for a large share of this table: it supplies the proof rule for the prior convictions that drive the grading in (2)(a), (2)(b), (4), and (6). DHSMV records showing a prior DUI conviction are sufficient BY THEMSELVES to establish that prior. The presumption is rebuttable -- the evidence 'may be contradicted or rebutted by other evidence' and is weighed along with any other evidence. Assigns no degree, but no prior-conviction trigger in this section can be assessed without it.
rows.quote: If the records of the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles show that the defendant has been previously convicted of the offense of driving under the influence, that evidence is sufficient by itself to establish that prior conviction for driving under the influence. However, such evidence may be contradicted or rebutted by other evidence. This presumption may be considered along with any other evidence presented in deciding whether the defendant has been previously convicted of the offense of driving under the influence.

rows.trigger: Introductory language of subsection (13). Gating rule: where circuit court personnel or the sheriff do not immobilize vehicles, ONLY immobilization agencies meeting the conditions of this subsection may immobilize vehicles in that judicial circuit. PARTY: immobilization agencies, not the DUI defendant (scope retyped to null on repair; party identity is off the typed vocabulary and lives here in prose). This is the provision that (6)(d) cross-references when it requires the impoundment order to list qualifying agencies. Assigns no degree itself; the criminal sanction is in (13)(c).
rows.quote: If personnel of the circuit court or the sheriff do not immobilize vehicles, only immobilization agencies that meet the conditions of this subsection shall immobilize vehicles in that judicial circuit.

rows.trigger: Supplies the ENTIRE substance of the offense that (13)(c) criminalizes: (13)(c) punishes 'a person who violates paragraph (a)' and says nothing about what paragraph (a) requires; without this row the elements of that first degree misdemeanor are nowhere in the table. PARTY: immobilization agencies and the persons they assign to immobilize vehicles (scope retyped to null on repair; party identity is off the typed vocabulary and lives here in prose). Subparagraph 1 imposes affidavit and recordkeeping duties on the agency: verifiable experience, accurate and complete records of payments, court orders, and all relevant documents kept for at least 3 years, and employment only of persons meeting subparagraph 2. Subparagraph 2 sets five disqualifiers for the individual who immobilizes a vehicle, covering adjudicated incapacity or involuntary mental health placement, chronic alcohol abuse or a DUI conviction within 2 years, controlled substance commitment or conviction, any unrestored felony, and citizenship or work authorization. Compliance is 'strict.' Assigns no degree itself.
rows.quote: The immobilization agency responsible for immobilizing vehicles in that judicial circuit shall be subject to strict compliance with all of the following conditions and restrictions:1. Any immobilization agency engaged in the business of immobilizing vehicles shall provide to the clerk of the court a signed affidavit attesting that the agency:a. Has verifiable experience in immobilizing vehicles;b. Maintains accurate and complete records of all payments for the immobilization, copies of all documents pertaining to the court’s order of impoundment or immobilization, and any other documents relevant to each immobilization. Such records must be maintained by the immobilization agency for at least 3 years; and c. Employs and assigns persons to immobilize vehicles that meet the requirements established in subparagraph 2. 2. The person who immobilizes a vehicle must:a. Not have been adjudicated incapacitated under s. 744.331, or a similar statute in another state, unless his or her capacity has been judicially restored; involuntarily placed in a treatment facility for the mentally ill under chapter 394, or a similar law in any other state, unless his or her competency has been judicially restored; or diagnosed as having an incapacitating mental illness unless a psychologist or psychiatrist licensed in this state certifies that he or she does not currently suffer from the mental illness.b. Not be a chronic and habitual user of alcoholic beverages to the extent that his or her normal faculties are impaired; not have been committed under chapter 397, former chapter 396, or a similar law in any other state; not have been found to be a habitual offender under s. 856.011(3), or a similar law in any other state; or not have had any convictions under this section, or a similar law in any other state, within 2 years before the affidavit is submitted.c. Not have been committed for controlled substance abuse or have been found guilty of a crime under chapter 893, or a similar law in any other state, relating to controlled substances in any other state.d. Not have been found guilty of or entered a plea of guilty or nolo contendere to, regardless of adjudication, or been convicted of a felony, unless his or her civil rights have been restored.e. Be a citizen or legal resident alien of the United States or have been granted authorization to seek employment in this country by the United States Bureau of Citizenship and Immigration Services.

rows.trigger: Mandatory FDLE state criminal history check by the immobilization agency on each person hired to immobilize a vehicle, to verify the felony disqualifier in sub-subparagraph (a)2.d. PARTY: immobilization agencies (scope retyped to null on repair; party identity is off the typed vocabulary and lives here in prose). Note the check is required only as to (a)2.d., not as to the other four disqualifiers in (a)2. Also note that (13)(c) criminalizes violations of paragraph (a) only, so a failure to run this (b) check is not itself made a crime by (13)(c). Assigns no degree.
rows.quote: The immobilization agency shall conduct a state criminal history check through the Florida Department of Law Enforcement to ensure that the person hired to immobilize a vehicle meets the requirements in sub-subparagraph (a)2.d.

rows.trigger: A SEPARATE OFFENSE BURIED IN A PROCEDURAL SUBSECTION, and it does not apply to the DUI defendant at all. PARTY: it reaches immobilization agencies and the persons they assign to immobilize vehicles -- NOT the DUI defendant. SCOPE RETYPED ON REPAIR: an earlier repair wrote that party identity into the scope field, but the typed vocabulary (dwelling/item/prior/victim/place) has no value for party identity, and an off-vocabulary string defeats the field's sole mechanical use; scope is therefore null and the who-it-reaches warning lives here in prose. It criminalizes violation of the recordkeeping, experience, affidavit, and personnel-qualification conditions in 316.193(13)(a) -- see the (13)(a) row for the elements. It reaches violations of paragraph (a) only, not the (b) criminal-history-check duty. A reader scanning only the grading subsections (2), (3), and (4) will never see that this section assigns a degree in subsection (13). Not ranked in the F.S. 921.0022 chart, which covers felonies only.
rows.quote: A person who violates paragraph (a) commits a misdemeanor of the first degree, punishable as provided in s. 775.082 or s. 775.083.

rows.trigger: Definitions, and note the scope: 'As used in this chapter' -- chapter 316 as a whole, not merely this section. Defines 'immobilization,' 'immobilizing,' or 'immobilize' (steering wheel antitheft device, tire lock or wheel clamp, or a governmental agency taking the license tag and registration), 'immobilization agency' (any entity meeting all the conditions of subsection (13)), 'impoundment,' 'impounding,' or 'impound' (storing the vehicle at a storage facility with control, supervision, and responsibility over it), and 'person' (which here means any business entity as well as an individual). These are the controlling definitions for the (6) impoundment and immobilization consequences and for the (13) offense. Note that the broad entity definition of 'person' in (14)(d) is what lets the (13)(c) misdemeanor reach an immobilization agency and not only an individual.
rows.quote: As used in this chapter, the term:(a) “Immobilization,” “immobilizing,” or “immobilize” means the act of installing a vehicle antitheft device on the steering wheel of a vehicle, the act of placing a tire lock or wheel clamp on a vehicle, or a governmental agency’s act of taking physical possession of the license tag and vehicle registration rendering a vehicle legally inoperable to prevent any person from operating the vehicle pursuant to an order of impoundment or immobilization under subsection (6).(b) “Immobilization agency” or “immobilization agencies” means any person, firm, company, agency, organization, partnership, corporation, association, trust, or other business entity of any kind whatsoever that meets all of the conditions of subsection (13).(c) “Impoundment,” “impounding,” or “impound” means the act of storing a vehicle at a storage facility pursuant to an order of impoundment or immobilization under subsection (6) where the person impounding the vehicle exercises control, supervision, and responsibility over the vehicle.(d) “Person” means any individual, firm, company, agency, organization, partnership, corporation, association, trust, or other business entity of any kind whatsoever.

unread: Nothing within F.S. 316.193 was left unread on this repair pass. I re-fetched the official 2025 text from flsenate.gov myself (curl, markup stripped) and read subsections (1) through (14) start to finish, including all four unnumbered flush paragraphs (the one closing (2)(a), the one closing (3), the one sitting between (4)(b)2. and (4)(c), and the one closing (6)), the History note, and both editor Notes. Every provision in the section has a row.

F.S. 921.0022 -- NOT read start to finish. I re-fetched it this pass and located every '316.193' occurrence in my extraction, then read the matching chart rows against the enclosing LEVEL headers. All six level assignments in this table were verified by my own reading: 316.193(2)(b) 3rd conviction in the LEVEL 3 block; 316.193(2)(b) 4th or subsequent in LEVEL 6; (3)(c)2. in LEVEL 7; (3)(c)3.a. in LEVEL 8; (3)(c)3.b. and (3)(c)3.c. in LEVEL 9. Several other hits in the chart are s. 316.1935 (fleeing or eluding), a different offense sharing the '316.193' substring, and were not imported. The remainder of the chart was not read.

F.S. 921.0024 -- not read. The sentencing points that attach to each offense severity level are therefore unverified here, and this table makes no claim about the numeric relationship between levels; they are ordinal chart placements only.

F.S. 775.082, 775.083, 775.084 -- not read. Every degree in this table is 'punishable as provided in' these sections, so the actual years and fines behind each degree are unverified here. Because these are unread, this table makes NO claim about their contents -- in particular no claim about how 775.082 would classify the direct 6-month and 9-month terms in 316.193(2)(a)2., which this section leaves ungraded on its face.
F.S. 316.1933 -- not read. Supplies the controlling definition of 'serious bodily injury' for 316.193(3)(c)2.
F.S. 775.021(5) -- not read. Supplies the controlling definition of 'unborn child' for 316.193(3)(c)3.
F.S. 316.062 -- not read. Supplies the give-information-and-render-aid duty that is element (II) of 316.193(3)(c)3.b.
F.S. 327.35(3)(a)3.c., 782.071, 782.072 -- not read. These are the qualifying prior convictions that elevate DUI manslaughter to a first degree felony under 316.193(3)(c)3.c.
F.S. 327.35, former 316.1931, former 860.01, former 316.028 -- not read. These define part of what counts as a 'previous conviction' under the flush language closing subsection (6).

F.S. 322.292 (DUI program licensure), 893.03 (Schedules I-V), and chapter 397 (substance abuse licensure) -- not read. All three are load-bearing for the mandatory probation, education, evaluation, and treatment conditions in 316.193(5).

F.S. 316.1938 (interlock device approval), 322.28(2)(a)2. and (2)(a)3. (license revocation), 322.2615 (administrative rulings), 316.1937 and 322.2715 (interlock for second or subsequent offenders, expressly overridden by (6)(j)1.), 713.78 (liens for towing and storage, incorporated wholesale by (6)(k)), 28.24 (clerk fees, (6)(l)), 877.111, chapter 893, 744.331, chapter 394, chapter 397, former chapter 396, 856.011(3), and Fla. R. Crim. P. 3.220 -- all cross-referenced by 316.193 and none of them read.

Case law construing any provision in this section -- not consulted. Three questions are unresolved on the face of the statute and would need it: whether the permissive 'may be not less than $2,000' fine floor in 316.193(2)(b)3. is treated as mandatory; whether the 'only the instant offense' rule in the subsection (4) flush language extends to the minor-passenger trigger, which that sentence does not mention; and whether the residential-treatment service option in (6)(m), which on its face reaches 'a term of imprisonment' under this section without carve-out, is in practice available against the DUI manslaughter 4-year mandatory minimum.

775.084.title: Violent career criminals; habitual felony offenders and habitual violent felony offenders; three-time violent felony offenders; definitions; procedure; enhanced penalties or mandatory minimum prison terms.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added as a row; previously existed only as prose inside the (4)(a) triggers. Habitual felony offender definition, the eligibility gate for the three penalty rows at (4)(a)1.-3. Five conjunctive findings: two or more prior felonies in this state or other qualified offenses per (1)(e); timing under 2.a. (committed while serving a sentence or supervision imposed for a prior felony or qualified offense) or 2.b. (within 5 years of the last prior conviction or of release, whichever is later); the s. 893.13 carve-out at 3., which disqualifies BOTH the current felony AND one of the two priors if either is a purchase-or-possession controlled substance offense; no pardon at 4.; no prior set aside in postconviction at 5. Predicate counting is expanded by (2) (withheld adjudication counts as a conviction) and contracted by (5) (priors must have been sentenced separately and sequentially). Note the contrast with (1)(b): this paragraph counts felonies simpliciter, with no attempt or conspiracy language in subparagraph 1.
rows.quote: “Habitual felony offender” means a defendant for whom the court may impose an extended term of imprisonment, as provided in paragraph (4)(a), if it finds that: 1. The defendant has previously been convicted of any combination of two or more felonies in this state or other qualified offenses. 2. The felony for which the defendant is to be sentenced was committed: a. While the defendant was serving a prison sentence or other sentence, or court-ordered or lawfully imposed supervision that is imposed as a result of a prior conviction for a felony or other qualified offense; or b. Within 5 years of the date of the conviction of the defendant’s last prior felony or other qualified offense, or within 5 years of the defendant’s release from a prison sentence, probation, community control, control release, conditional release, parole or court-ordered or lawfully imposed supervision or other sentence that is imposed as a result of a prior conviction for a felony or other qualified offense, whichever is later. 3. The felony for which the defendant is to be sentenced, and one of the two prior felony convictions, is not a violation of s. 893.13 relating to the purchase or the possession of a controlled substance. 4. The defendant has not received a pardon for any felony or other qualified offense that is necessary for the operation of this paragraph. 5. A conviction of a felony or other qualified offense necessary to the operation of this paragraph has not been set aside in any postconviction proceeding.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added as a row; previously recited only inside the (4)(b)1. trigger. Habitual violent felony offender definition, the eligibility gate for the three penalty rows at (4)(b)1.-3. Requires one or more prior convictions for a felony OR AN ATTEMPT OR CONSPIRACY to commit a felony from the closed fifteen-item list at 1.a.-o., plus the 2.a.-b. timing (serving a sentence for an enumerated felony, or within 5 years of that conviction or release, whichever is later), 3. no pardon on the ground of innocence, and 4. no conviction set aside. Predicate counting governed by (2) and (5). ASYMMETRY previously lost and now recorded: this paragraph counts an attempt OR CONSPIRACY to commit an enumerated felony, while (1)(c)1. counts attempts only, never conspiracies, and (1)(a)1. counts neither. A conspiracy-to-commit-robbery prior qualifies a defendant here but contributes nothing under (1)(c).
rows.quote: “Habitual violent felony offender” means a defendant for whom the court may impose an extended term of imprisonment, as provided in paragraph (4)(b), if it finds that: 1. The defendant has previously been convicted of a felony or an attempt or conspiracy to commit a felony and one or more of such convictions was for: a. Arson; b. Sexual battery; c. Robbery; d. Kidnapping; e. Aggravated child abuse; f. Aggravated abuse of an elderly person or disabled adult; g. Aggravated assault with a deadly weapon; h. Murder; i. Manslaughter; j. Aggravated manslaughter of an elderly person or disabled adult; k. Aggravated manslaughter of a child; l. Unlawful throwing, placing, or discharging of a destructive device or bomb; m. Armed burglary; n. Aggravated battery; or o. Aggravated stalking. 2. The felony for which the defendant is to be sentenced was committed: a. While the defendant was serving a prison sentence or other sentence, or court-ordered or lawfully imposed supervision that is imposed as a result of a prior conviction for an enumerated felony; or b. Within 5 years of the date of the conviction of the last prior enumerated felony, or within 5 years of the defendant’s release from a prison sentence, probation, community control, control release, conditional release, parole, or court-ordered or lawfully imposed supervision or other sentence that is imposed as a result of a prior conviction for an enumerated felony, whichever is later. 3. The defendant has not received a pardon on the ground of innocence for any crime that is necessary for the operation of this paragraph. 4. A conviction of a crime necessary to the operation of this paragraph has not been set aside in any postconviction proceeding.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added as a row, with the 1.a.-r. list now recited IN FULL rather than described as a delta against the (1)(b) list. Three-time violent felony offender definition, the eligibility gate for the four penalty rows at (4)(c)1.a.-d. Requires two or more prior adult convictions for committing OR ATTEMPTING (attempts only; no conspiracy, unlike (1)(b)1.) any offense on the eighteen-item list at 1.a.-r., which is the (1)(b) list plus home invasion/robbery (p.), carjacking (q.), and the out-of-jurisdiction analogue clause (r.). Under 2., the CURRENT felony must itself be one of the offenses enumerated in 1.a.-q. (a.-q., not a.-r., so a pure out-of-jurisdiction offense cannot be the current offense) with serving-a-sentence or within-5-years timing, and the timing predicates reference the broader a.-r. list. Plus 3. no pardon on the ground of innocence and 4. no conviction set aside. Predicate counting governed by (2) and (5). This is the one category with no protection-of-the-public escape, no (4)(j) conditional release, no (4)(k)1. gain-time, and the absolute (4)(k)3. expiration-of-sentence rule.
rows.quote: “Three-time violent felony offender” means a defendant for whom the court must impose a mandatory minimum term of imprisonment, as provided in paragraph (4)(c), if it finds that: 1. The defendant has previously been convicted as an adult two or more times of a felony, or an attempt to commit a felony, and two or more of such convictions were for committing, or attempting to commit, any of the following offenses or combination thereof: a. Arson; b. Sexual battery; c. Robbery; d. Kidnapping; e. Aggravated child abuse; f. Aggravated abuse of an elderly person or disabled adult; g. Aggravated assault with a deadly weapon; h. Murder; i. Manslaughter; j. Aggravated manslaughter of an elderly person or disabled adult; k. Aggravated manslaughter of a child; l. Unlawful throwing, placing, or discharging of a destructive device or bomb; m. Armed burglary; n. Aggravated battery; o. Aggravated stalking; p. Home invasion/robbery; q. Carjacking; or r. An offense which is in violation of a law of any other jurisdiction if the elements of the offense are substantially similar to the elements of any felony offense enumerated in sub-subparagraphs a.-q., or an attempt to commit any such felony offense. 2. The felony for which the defendant is to be sentenced is one of the felonies enumerated in sub-subparagraphs 1.a.-q. and was committed: a. While the defendant was serving a prison sentence or other sentence imposed as a result of a prior conviction for any offense enumerated in sub-subparagraphs 1.a.-r.; or b. Within 5 years after the date of the conviction of the last prior offense enumerated in sub-subparagraphs 1.a.-r., or within 5 years after the defendant’s release from a prison sentence, probation, community control, or other sentence imposed as a result of a prior conviction for any offense enumerated in sub-subparagraphs 1.a.-r., whichever is later. 3. The defendant has not received a pardon on the ground of innocence for any crime that is necessary for the operation of this paragraph. 4. A conviction of a crime necessary to the operation of this paragraph has not been set aside in any postconviction proceeding.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added as a row; previously recited only inside the (4)(d)1. trigger. Violent career criminal definition, the eligibility gate for the three penalty rows at (4)(d)1.-3. Five conjunctive findings: 1. three or more prior adult convictions in this state or qualified offenses per (1)(e) from the list at 1.a.-g.; 2. prior incarceration in a state or federal prison; 3. the primary offense itself enumerated in subparagraph 1., committed on or after October 1, 1995, with serving-a-sentence or within-5-years timing; 4. no pardon; 5. no conviction set aside. Predicate counting governed by (2) and (5). CRITICAL and previously buried: the predicate list is NOT a closed list of violent named offenses. Its FIRST item, 1.a., incorporates the open-ended, any-degree forcible felony class of s. 776.08 (see the dedicated (1)(d)1.a. row), and its LAST item, 1.g., admits bare firearm possession at any felony degree (see the dedicated (1)(d)1.g. row). Only items b.-f. are bounded named statutes.
rows.quote: “Violent career criminal” means a defendant for whom the court must impose imprisonment pursuant to paragraph (4)(d), if it finds that: 1. The defendant has previously been convicted as an adult three or more times for an offense in this state or other qualified offense that is: a. Any forcible felony, as described in s. 776.08; b. Aggravated stalking, as described in s. 784.048(3) and (4); c. Aggravated child abuse, as described in s. 827.03(2)(a); d. Aggravated abuse of an elderly person or disabled adult, as described in s. 825.102(2); e. Lewd or lascivious battery, lewd or lascivious molestation, lewd or lascivious conduct, or lewd or lascivious exhibition, as described in s. 800.04 or s. 847.0135(5); f. Escape, as described in s. 944.40; or g. A felony violation of chapter 790 involving the use or possession of a firearm. 2. The defendant has been incarcerated in a state prison or a federal prison. 3. The primary felony offense for which the defendant is to be sentenced is a felony enumerated in subparagraph 1. and was committed on or after October 1, 1995, and: a. While the defendant was serving a prison sentence or other sentence, or court-ordered or lawfully imposed supervision that is imposed as a result of a prior conviction for an enumerated felony; or b. Within 5 years after the conviction of the last prior enumerated felony, or within 5 years after the defendant’s release from a prison sentence, probation, community control, control release, conditional release, parole, or court-ordered or lawfully imposed supervision or other sentence that is imposed as a result of a prior conviction for an enumerated felony, whichever is later. 4. The defendant has not received a pardon for any felony or other qualified offense that is necessary for the operation of this paragraph. 5. A conviction of a felony or other qualified offense necessary to the operation of this paragraph has not been set aside in any postconviction proceeding.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added; the auditor's headline NO-LOWER-BOUND finding, previously parked in unread as an unopened cross-reference. The first item of the (1)(d)1. predicate list, and the only one that is not a bounded named statute. s. 776.08, opened and read for this repair, defines forcible felony as a named list (treason; murder; manslaughter; sexual battery; carjacking; home-invasion robbery; robbery; burglary; arson; kidnapping; aggravated assault; aggravated battery; aggravated stalking; aircraft piracy; unlawful throwing, placing, or discharging of a destructive device or bomb) that CLOSES with a residual clause: “and any other felony which involves the use or threat of physical force or violence against any individual.” The residual clause states no degree floor, so a third degree felony involving the use or threat of physical force counts as a violent career criminal predicate, and the class is open-ended rather than enumerated. This is the F.S. 775.082(9)(a)1.o pattern reproduced one level down through an incorporated cross-reference, and inverted in position: the unbounded item leads the list while the bounded named statutes at b.-g. follow it. It materially widens the predicate pool for all three rows at (4)(d)1.-3., including the 30-year and 10-year mandatory minimums at (4)(d)2. and (4)(d)3.
rows.quote: Any forcible felony, as described in s. 776.08;

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added; the auditor's second no-lower-bound finding. The last item of the (1)(d)1. predicate list carries no degree floor and no use-of-force element: A FELONY violation of chapter 790 involving the use OR POSSESSION of a firearm. Bare possession, at the bottom of the felony ladder, counts as one of the three predicates that make a defendant a violent career criminal. A defendant with three third-degree felon-in-possession convictions under chapter 790 satisfies (1)(d)1. without any prior act of violence, subject to the remaining (1)(d)2.-5. findings. The word “violent” in the category name does not bound this item, and the prior table's characterization of the (1)(d) list as violent priors was wrong as to this sub-subparagraph.
rows.quote: A felony violation of chapter 790 involving the use or possession of a firearm.

rows.trigger: Cross-cutting predicate definition, not a penalty. Defines "qualified offense," the out-of-state/federal/foreign conviction that counts as a predicate. It feeds the (1)(a) habitual felony offender predicate ("two or more felonies in this state or other qualified offenses") and the (1)(d) violent career criminal predicate ("an offense in this state or other qualified offense"), so it silently widens the prior-conviction pool for the (4)(a) and (4)(d) rows. Note the substantive limits it carries: elements AND penalties must be substantially similar to a Florida offense, and the foreign offense must have been punishable by death or imprisonment exceeding 1 year at the time of commission.
rows.quote: “Qualified offense” means any offense, substantially similar in elements and penalties to an offense in this state, which is in violation of a law of any other jurisdiction, whether that of another state, the District of Columbia, the United States or any possession or territory thereof, or any foreign jurisdiction, that was punishable under the law of such jurisdiction at the time of its commission by the defendant by death or imprisonment exceeding 1 year.

rows.trigger: Cross-cutting predicate expansion that governs every penalty row in subsection (4). It is not derivable from the (1)(a)-(1)(d) definitional text, which speaks only of a defendant "previously convicted." A withheld adjudication (probation or community control without an adjudication of guilt) is not a conviction under ordinary Florida usage, and this subsection overrides that for all four categories: habitual felony offender, habitual violent felony offender, three-time violent felony offender, and violent career criminal. It applies "for the purposes of this section," so its reach is the whole section. Read together with (5), which cuts the other way by requiring the priors to have been sentenced separately and sequentially.
rows.quote: For the purposes of this section, the placing of a person on probation or community control without an adjudication of guilt shall be treated as a prior conviction.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added; previously disclosed in unread as pure procedure with no row. The separate-proceeding requirement and its five procedural incidents for habitual felony offender and habitual violent felony offender sentencing: 1. mandatory presentence investigation; 2. written notice to the defendant and counsel in time to prepare a submission; 3. open court with confrontation, cross-examination, and counsel, except the presentence investigation; 4. findings by a preponderance, appealable to the extent normally applicable to similar findings; 5. fingerprinting under s. 921.241. Contrast (3)(c), which omits the presentence-investigation requirement and narrows appealability to (3)(d).
rows.quote: In a separate proceeding, the court shall determine if the defendant is a habitual felony offender or a habitual violent felony offender. The procedure shall be as follows: 1. The court shall obtain and consider a presentence investigation prior to the imposition of a sentence as a habitual felony offender or a habitual violent felony offender. 2. Written notice shall be served on the defendant and the defendant’s attorney a sufficient time prior to the entry of a plea or prior to the imposition of sentence in order to allow the preparation of a submission on behalf of the defendant. 3. Except as provided in subparagraph 1., all evidence presented shall be presented in open court with full rights of confrontation, cross-examination, and representation by counsel. 4. Each of the findings required as the basis for such sentence shall be found to exist by a preponderance of the evidence and shall be appealable to the extent normally applicable to similar findings. 5. For the purpose of identification of a habitual felony offender or a habitual violent felony offender, the court shall fingerprint the defendant pursuant to s. 921.241.

rows.trigger: REPAIR (quote defect fixed): the prior quote stopped at "...not necessary for the protection of the public" with no ellipsis, omitting two of the subparagraph's three sentences while the trigger asserted their content. The full subparagraph is now quoted. Converts the permissive "may sentence" of (4)(a) and (4)(b) into a mandatory sanction for offenses committed on or after October 1, 1995, subject to one escape: the court may decline if it finds the sentence is not necessary for the protection of the public, in which case it must provide written reasons (or a transcript of orally stated reasons filed within 7 days) and report them monthly to the Office of Economic and Demographic Research. Two preconditions gate the mandate: the state attorney must PURSUE the sanction, and the court must find the (1) criteria met in a separate proceeding. Governs all six rows at (4)(a)1.-3. and (4)(b)1.-3. Notably absent for the three-time violent felony offender, see (3)(b)6.
rows.quote: For an offense committed on or after October 1, 1995, if the state attorney pursues a habitual felony offender sanction or a habitual violent felony offender sanction against the defendant and the court, in a separate proceeding pursuant to this paragraph, determines that the defendant meets the criteria under subsection (1) for imposing such sanction, the court must sentence the defendant as a habitual felony offender or a habitual violent felony offender, subject to imprisonment pursuant to this section unless the court finds that such sentence is not necessary for the protection of the public. If the court finds that it is not necessary for the protection of the public to sentence the defendant as a habitual felony offender or a habitual violent felony offender, the court shall provide written reasons; a written transcript of orally stated reasons is permissible, if filed by the court within 7 days after the date of sentencing. Each month, the court shall submit to the Office of Economic and Demographic Research of the Legislature the written reasons or transcripts in each case in which the court determines not to sentence a defendant as a habitual felony offender or a habitual violent felony offender as provided in this subparagraph.

rows.trigger: REPAIR: added; previously disclosed in unread with no row. The separate-proceeding requirement and its five procedural incidents for three-time violent felony offender sentencing, parallel to (3)(a)1.-5.: mandatory presentence investigation, written notice, open court with confrontation and counsel, preponderance standard with findings appealable to the extent normally applicable, and fingerprinting under s. 921.241.
rows.quote: In a separate proceeding, the court shall determine if the defendant is a three-time violent felony offender. The procedure shall be as follows: 1. The court shall obtain and consider a presentence investigation prior to the imposition of a sentence as a three-time violent felony offender. 2. Written notice shall be served on the defendant and the defendant’s attorney a sufficient time prior to the entry of a plea or prior to the imposition of sentence in order to allow the preparation of a submission on behalf of the defendant. 3. Except as provided in subparagraph 1., all evidence presented shall be presented in open court with full rights of confrontation, cross-examination, and representation by counsel. 4.
